summary: The build can start: the machine has the Python runtime, a connected DocumentDB MCP server (profile `default`) pointed at a reachable DocumentDB cluster, az CLI signed-in, node/npx for agent skills, and the DocumentDB agent skills that the sample needs. Key factual confusions (resource types, CLI groups, billing model, auth modes, vector / search index commands, local dev image and driver/ODM tension with Beanie) were discovered and corrected against Microsoft Learn and the installed DocumentDB skills. Missing accelerators (DocumentDB Agent Kit) and local tools (mongosh, azd, bicep, terraform) would speed work but are not blockers; driver/ODM choices and embedding/LLM model selection remain decisions the builder must make before coding.
summary_points: All required data‑plane tools to verify and run the sample exist: documentdb MCP server (connection profile `default`) is available and the target DB sample_customer_360_07 exists (empty).

Core runtime is present (python/pip, node/npx, docker) and the DocumentDB agent skills (connection, driver, vector-search, full-text-search, deployment, local-deploy, etc.) are installed and were used to ground facts.

Multiple cold answers were incorrect because the model mixed this new 'Azure DocumentDB' product with older Cosmos DB (RU) or Amazon DocumentDB or generic MongoDB conventions — fixable but important for code (connection string, billing model, CLI commands, index creation calls, auth methods, local image/port, vector & FTS APIs).

The main practical friction for the sample: Beanie historically uses Motor while the documentdb-driver guidance recommends PyMongo's AsyncMongoClient for new async code — the builder must pick which approach (use Motor + Beanie as-is, or adapt to AsyncPyMongo) and document the choice.
Missing accelerators (DocumentDB Agent Kit) and developer tools (mongosh, azd, bicep, terraform) are useful but optional; add them to the environment to speed build/verification.

Information the sample must decide (embedding model & dimension, LLM provider/model, exact index parameters for selected embedding dims) is not answered by skills/docs and must be set by the builder before implementing indexes and embeddings.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: databaseAccounts (i.e. Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).
confusions.grounded_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for this product: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (the new mongoClusters resource).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer describes the older Cosmos DB account resource (Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) used by Cosmos DB (including the MongoDB API variant). Azure DocumentDB is a separate vCore-based product that uses the new resource type `Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters`.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb create quickstarts (older Cosmos DB guidance)

confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts (az cosmosdb) templates or CLI commands would create or target the wrong service (Cosmos DB RU model), causing billing, API surface and connection-string mismatches. Provisioning / index-management calls would fail or be inapplicable.
improvements: On the Azure DocumentDB overview and quickstart pages, add a clear, one-line statement: "This product uses resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts)" and include example az documentdb mongocluster CLI commands.
Add a deprecation/clarity banner on older Cosmos DB-for-Mongo pages explaining the difference and linking to mongoClusters docs.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in Azure CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create a Mongo-compatible account: az cosmosdb create --name MyDocDbAccount --resource-group MyRG --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2 --default-consistency-level Session
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct CLI group is az documentdb mongocluster (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create / az documentdb mongocluster list); the az CLI includes an `az documentdb` command module for this product.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer references the older az cosmosdb command group used for Cosmos DB accounts (the RU-based product). Azure DocumentDB has its own az documentdb command group with mongocluster subcommands.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb CLI docs (for Cosmos DB accounts)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb commands would target the wrong control-plane API and not expose the mongoClusters create/update arguments; CLI scripts in the sample would fail or create different resources.
improvements: Update the 'Create cluster' quickstart and the CLI reference to highlight `az documentdb mongocluster` as the preferred command group and show one-line examples in the landing page.
Add a short note in the az cosmosdb docs explaining the distinct `az documentdb` command group for vCore-based DocumentDB clusters.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: resource of type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account for the account; ancillary resources include azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database and azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection.
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep/Terraform resource type for this service is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (Bicep modules and Terraform AVMs target mongoClusters); Terraform AzAPI/azurerm exposes azurerm_mongo_cluster / avm modules for this resource (or the API-backed azurerm resource variant).

grounding_links.title: Terraform AVM for Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) / mongo-cluster

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflects older Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts / azurerm_cosmosdb_account) resource types used by Cosmos DB's Mongo API. The vCore DocumentDB product uses the dedicated mongoClusters resource and the AVM/provider modules reflect that.

confusion_sources.title: azurerm_cosmosdb_account docs (older Cosmos DB Terraform resource)

confusions.build_risk: Using the databaseAccounts / azurerm_cosmosdb_account resource in IaC would deploy the wrong control-plane resource and produce a different (RU-based) account; index and billing models would differ.
improvements: Add a 'Bicep/Terraform quick compare' section on the DocumentDB landing page that clearly lists `Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters` and links to the AVM Terraform module and a canonical Bicep template.
Deprecate or mark as 'Cosmos DB (RU)' the pages that still show databaseAccounts as the only code example for Mongo-compatible deployments.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB URI forms. Host suffix: <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com (or SRV: <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com). Port for direct (non-SRV) TLS connections: 10255. Examples: SRV form: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB cluster connection strings use mongodb+srv scheme against hosts like `<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com` (or `<cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com`), TLS must be enabled (tls=true), recommended authMechanisms include SCRAM-SHA-256 for key-based auth or MONGODB-OIDC / MONGODB-AUTH mechanisms for Microsoft Entra ID, and `retrywrites=false` is recommended. The port 10255 and host suffix `*.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255` reflect older Cosmos DB Mongo endpoints and do not apply here.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver (Python example)
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer describes connection string forms historically used by Cosmos DB's Mongo endpoint (`*.mongo.cosmos.azure.com` and port 10255). Azure DocumentDB uses different host names (mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com / global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and emphasizes SRV/tls plus specific auth mechanisms (MONGODB-OIDC for Entra ID).

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB Mongo quickstarts that use <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com and 10255

confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses the wrong host suffix/port or wrong auth options, clients will fail to connect or attempt unsupported auth/replica-set behaviour; e.g., using `replicaSet=globaldb` and port 10255 could break connections to mongoClusters.
improvements: On the 'how to connect' page, add an explicit example and recommended connection string for `az documentdb` clusters (SRV with `.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com`, tls=true, retrywrites=false, authMechanism examples).
Add a migration-caveat section on older connection-string examples showing the new host/port differences and the MONGODB-OIDC form when using Entra ID.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is primarily billed as Request Units per second (RU/s) for Cosmos DB accounts (including Mongo API). You can provision fixed RU/s, use autoscale RU, and some regions/accounts support serverless or consumption options.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore product) bills by compute tier (vCores — M10, M20, M30, ...) and provisioned storage per shard. It does NOT use Cosmos DB RU/s billing for this product; RU/s is the billing model for Cosmos DB (RU-based) variants.

grounding_links.title: FAQ: How does Azure DocumentDB relate to Azure Cosmos DB?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer describes Cosmos DB's RU/s billing model (used by Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) accounts). Azure DocumentDB is the separate vCore-based product with M-series compute tiers and per-shard storage billing.
confusions.build_risk: Picking an RU/s-driven architecture or expecting autoscale RU features would lead to incorrect provisioning and cost expectations; index/throughput tuning guides differ between RU and vCore models.
improvements: Update the Azure DocumentDB pricing page to include a clear, top-of-page comparison to Cosmos DB RU billing: 'Use Azure DocumentDB (vCore) — billed by compute tier + storage — not RU/s'.
Add a short example cost-calculation snippet that shows M30 + storage costs vs equivalent RU configuration so builders pick correct sizing defaults.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: MongoDB API on Azure Cosmos DB primarily uses SCRAM-style username/password authentication where the username is the database user (often <db>@<account>) and the password is the account key. Historically Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) auth is not supported for the MongoDB wire API ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports multiple auth modes: native SCRAM (username/password keyed to a cluster admin or db user) and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) for data-plane authentication. Entra ID auth uses MONGODB-OIDC / OIDC connection-string forms (client-id as username, OIDC options/TOKEN_RESOURCE), see the 'Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control' docs.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID
az documentdb mongocluster create CLI: --auth-allowed-modes includes MicrosoftEntraID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer describes older Cosmos DB Mongo API limitations where AAD/OIDC support was limited. Azure DocumentDB's newer control-plane/engine exposes Entra ID / OIDC integration for data-plane auth and even documents how to construct OIDC connection URIs.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB Mongo pages that said AAD not supported for data-plane

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Entra ID is unsupported, they may hardcode keys or ignore managed-identity flows that customers want; conversely, if they use the OIDC form without following docs, connection attempts might fail.
improvements: On the 'how-to-connect' doc add explicit, copy-paste OIDC connection-string examples and a small walkthrough for registering/assigning managed identities used with Compass or drivers.
On 'az documentdb mongocluster create' docs, show `--auth-allowed-modes` examples enabling MicrosoftEntraID with a short note linking to the client-side OIDC string example.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (e.g. pymongo or motor for Python). There is no separate service-specific MongoDB driver — the official MongoDB drivers are used ... For Python async ODM, Beanie runs on motor and pydantic.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (PyMongo for sync, AsyncMongoClient for async where available) and the usual MongoDB ecosystem tools. The product docs and quickstarts show examples with the official MongoDB drivers. Note: DocumentDB driver/skill guidance recommends PyMongo's AsyncMongoClient for new async code. Beanie historically uses Motor; this creates a practical choice for the builder (use Motor with Beanie, or adapt to AsyncPyMongo if Beanie supports it). There is no separate, proprietary DocumentDB Mongo driver.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer is broadly correct that standard MongoDB drivers are used, but the builder-facing skill guidance recommends PyMongo's AsyncMongoClient for new async apps while Beanie historically depends on Motor — creating a practical conflict the builder must resolve.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder blindly follows Beanie + Motor without checking deprecation/compatibility, they might rely on a deprecated stack or miss driver-tuning guidance; conversely adapting Beanie to AsyncPyMongo without checking support will create runtime issues.
improvements: Add a short 'Python driver + ODM' guidance note in the sample or on the DocumentDB quickstart: 'If you pick Beanie, Motor is the simplest path; for new async code we recommend evaluating PyMongo AsyncMongoClient and confirming your ODM's compatibility. Include a short example for both flows in the samples repo.'
Add a 'Beanie compatibility note' on the Beanie sample: show a Motor-based example and an AsyncPyMongo-compatible snippet if adapter code exists.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Vector support ... exposes multiple index types such as HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. Example createIndex with { embedding: 'vector' } and algorithm: 'hnsw' ... dimensions: 1536 ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB's native vector support is exposed via the `cosmosSearch` vector index family; sub-types are `vector-diskann`, `vector-hnsw`, `vector-ivf`. Vector indexes and hybrid retrieval are created/managed through the search index APIs (createSearchIndexes / createSearchIndexes definition) and queried via `$search` + cosmosSearch rather than a straight `createIndex({embedding:'vector'}, ...)` Mongo shell call. Choose sub-type by scale (DiskANN for production larger sets; HNSW/IVF for smaller).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed the common 'createIndex' style seen in some MongoDB vendor extensions with DocumentDB's `createSearchIndexes`/`$search` vector approach; the index concept (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN) is correct, but the API to create and tune them is DocumentDB-specific (`createSearchIndexes` + `cosmosSearch` parameters), not the standard createIndex with 'algorithm' options.

confusion_sources.title: Community-style createIndex examples for vector extensions

confusions.build_risk: If the builder attempts to create vector indexes with the standard createIndex call, the operation will fail or create a non-functional index; queries expecting `$search`/cosmosSearch will not use the intended vector index.
improvements: On vector-search docs add an explicit, copy-paste example of `runCommand({ createSearchIndexes: ...})` that defines a `vector-diskann` index with `dimensions`, `similarity`, `lBuild` etc., and show the corresponding `$search` query example.
Deprecate any sample that uses generic createIndex for vectors and replace with createSearchIndexes examples and best-practice parameter guidance per index sub-type.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use MongoDB text indexes and $text where supported; for hybrid use Azure Cognitive Search or push documents to Azure Cognitive Search or use provider-exposed vector search.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides native full-text search via `createSearchIndexes` and the `$search` aggregation stage (BM25). For hybrid lexical+vector retrieval use the DocumentDB `cosmosSearch` + `$search` patterns and the documented Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) approach. Do not rely on community `$text` indexes as the DocumentDB search path; prefer createSearchIndexes + `$search`.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer applies common MongoDB patterns (`$text`) or the external-search integration approach (Azure Cognitive Search). DocumentDB exposes a richer internal search system (`createSearchIndexes` + `$search`) designed for BM25 scoring and hybrid combos with vector search.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses `$text` or offloads to Azure Cognitive Search unnecessarily, they will bypass integrated capabilities (BM25 + vector) and increase complexity and cost. Also `$text` may not be as feature-rich as DocumentDB's `$search`.
improvements: On the DocumentDB search docs, add a short 'why not $text?' explanation and side-by-side examples showing `createSearchIndexes` + `$search` vs `$text` to steer builders to the recommended path.
Add a hybrid-search recipe (BM25 + vector) with recommended parameter values for small and medium datasets.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supports specific MongoDB wire protocol versions and typically lags; common compatibility tags have been 3.6, 4.0, 4.2, 4.4, 5.0 and newer; some features not supported: server-side JS ($where), some aggregation stages, administrative commands, etc.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0, with about 99.03% of MongoDB operators supported. A small set of administrative commands and a handful of aggregation stages/operators may differ; the detailed compatibility pages list specifics — builders should run the compatibility assessment for precise migration checks.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (wire protocol versions supported)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer listed older compatibility versions and vague missing features; the authoritative docs list current supported wire protocol versions (5.0-8.0) and provide a detailed operator-by-operator compatibility table.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming an older wire protocol could cause unnecessary compatibility fixes or missing the fact that DocumentDB supports newer wire protocol versions; conversely assuming full parity without checking the compatibility table risks subtle runtime errors during migration.
improvements: Add a concise 'supported wire protocol versions' snippet in the quickstart landing page and link to the detailed compatibility matrix for the full operator list.
Provide a small checklist for the compatibility assessment in the migration quickstart to encourage running the VS Code extension early.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is a Cosmos DB emulator and for Mongo compatibility I would run the official MongoDB Docker image (mongo:7.0) on port 27017 and test there.
confusions.grounded_answer: For local development with Azure DocumentDB, run the provided DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) which exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 (and PostgreSQL on 9712). Using a plain mongo:7.0 image will not match DocumentDB-specific features like the gateway behaviour, search/vector APIs, or exact port/SSL requirements.

grounding_links.title: Local gateway image and ports (gateway on 10260)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer suggested using the generic MongoDB container (27017), which is common for MongoDB-centric projects; DocumentDB provides a specialized Gateway image and uses port 10260 for parity with the service internals.
confusions.build_risk: Testing against a plain mongo container may miss DocumentDB-specific behaviour (search API, vector index semantics, TLS/connection-string differences). The sample would pass locally but break when run against the real cluster.
improvements: Make the local-gateway example and docker-compose file easily discoverable in the samples repo and quickstart, emphasising port 10260 and TLS configuration, and providing a ready-to-run `docker-compose.local.yml` for the sample.
Add a 'how to run integration tests locally' snippet that shows using the gateway image with SKIP_INIT_DATA / INIT_DATA_PATH variables and the env-driven connection URI pattern.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change Feed is a Cosmos DB native capability (Core/SQL). Support for MongoDB-style change streams depends on the MongoDB compatibility level/version; historically MongoDB change streams were not supported on all compatibility versions.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB does support MongoDB-style change streams (resumable, with resume tokens) and also offers historical checkpoint/replay integration; for migrations and online replication, change streams are an expected path. Source clusters used for migration must have change streams enabled at the source side; DocumentDB supports change streams on the target (see change-stream docs).

grounding_links.title: Migration guidance: enable change streams on source

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer conflated Cosmos DB Core change feed and historic limitations of older Mongo API versions; the current DocumentDB product documents change-stream support explicitly and provides resume/historical options.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are unsupported they will choose offline migration or polling strategies unnecessarily; conversely assuming always-on historical stream replay without checking cluster features could oversubscribe resources.
improvements: Add a short 'change streams' quick example and the recommended production patterns (resumability with resume tokens, typical retention expectations) in the migration quickstart page.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: The documentdb MCP server (named 'documentdb' in the environment) provides data-plane inspection tools for Cosmos DB / DocumentDB resources. The general azure MCP server covers general Azure control-plane tasks but the specialized 'documentdb' MCP server is the one with collection/index inspectors and query plan tools for this service.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the `documentdb` MCP server provides the data-plane tools (query, aggregation, index management, explain). The general `azure` MCP server covers control-plane lookups but not the data-plane explain/index tools.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft originally called its NoSQL service DocumentDB; it evolved into and was rebranded/merged into Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB API became Cosmos DB's Core/SQL and other APIs). Microsoft DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is distinct from any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB. Also, be careful not to confuse Microsoft DocumentDB/Cosmos DB with Amazon DocumentDB (AWS).
confusions.grounded_answer: Historical naming is nuanced: the name 'DocumentDB' was used historically (the 2014–2017 service that became Azure Cosmos DB). The current product named 'Azure DocumentDB' (the vCore MongoDB-compatible offering) was formerly called 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' and was rebranded to Azure DocumentDB; it is distinct from the original DocumentDB/Cosmos DB and from Amazon DocumentDB. The open-source 'DocumentDB' engine underpins this product and is MIT-licensed.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (naming and history)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer compresses two separate historical naming events into one: the original 'DocumentDB' service became Cosmos DB long ago, while the newer vCore 'Cosmos DB for MongoDB' product was rebranded to 'Azure DocumentDB' more recently — a nuance easily lost.
confusions.build_risk: Naming confusion can cause the builder to pick wrong docs or CLI commands (Cosmos DB vs DocumentDB) and mis-explain the sample to users.
improvements: Add a short timeline on the overview page showing: original DocumentDB (2014→became Cosmos DB), Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) vs vCore offering, rebranding to Azure DocumentDB, and how each maps to resource types and billing models.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the MongoDB API the service is backed by Azure Cosmos DB's own storage and query engine which implements the MongoDB wire protocol rather than running the upstream MongoDB server. That means you use standard MongoDB drivers and most client code unchanged, but you must expect some server-side differences/limitations ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (not the upstream MongoDB server and not the classic Cosmos DB engine). It still implements the MongoDB wire protocol so standard MongoDB drivers and most client code work, but some admin commands and a small set of operators differ. The important effect on app code is: same driver usage but verify compatibility for advanced server-side features against the compatibility docs.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer implied the Cosmos DB engine underlies the service; in fact the vCore Azure DocumentDB product runs on the open-source DocumentDB engine, which is different from Cosmos DB's original engine — but the practical driver-compatibility outcome (use MongoDB drivers) remains similar.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming the Cosmos DB engine underlies the product could lead to using Cosmos DB-specific guidance (RU/s, databaseAccounts resource type) in code and IaC, which would be wrong for this product.
improvements: Clarify in the overview doc that Azure DocumentDB runs on the open-source DocumentDB engine and include a short note: 'driver usage is unchanged; check compatibility doc for edge cases.'

confusions.question: Which database name should the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database named sample_customer_360_07 for all sample-created collections and operations.
confusions.grounded_answer: Confirmed: the run-environment and sample instructions require using the database sample_customer_360_07. The documentdb MCP server lists that database (it exists and currently has no collections).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none

confusions.question: How should the sample read the cluster connection string and which client and ODM will it use?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime. Use an async Mongo client (motor) as the driver and Beanie ODM (which is built on motor and pydantic) for document modelling and persistence in the Python LangChain agent.
confusions.grounded_answer: Confirmed: read the cluster connection string from environment (the run environment instructs DOCUMENTDB_URI). For the driver/ODM: the official quickstarts show examples with standard MongoDB drivers (MongoClient/pymongo for sync); DocumentDB guidance recommends using PyMongo's AsyncMongoClient for new async code, while Beanie historically uses Motor. This is a practical choice the builder must make: either use Beanie + Motor (simple) or adapt to AsyncPyMongo (recommended by driver skill).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixes the sample environment requirement (DOCUMENTDB_URI) — which is correct — with a Motor+Beanie recommendation. The installed driver skill prefers AsyncPyMongo; Beanie historically uses Motor.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder blindly follows Beanie + Motor without confirming driver guidance, they may use a deprecated path or miss recommended tuning from documentdb-driver. If they flip to AsyncPyMongo they'd need to confirm Beanie compatibility or find an alternate ODM pattern.
improvements: Add a short note in the sample README: 'We use Beanie + Motor in this sample for simplicity; see the documentdb-driver skill for AsyncPyMongo guidance and an alternate approach.'
Update the agent-kit samples to include both a Beanie+Motor example and an AsyncPyMongo+ODM alternative (with conversion notes).

confusions.question: What collection and index plan will the sample create for storing enriched documents and embeddings?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a collection named customer_feedback, store embeddings in a field named embedding (array of floats). Create a vector index on embedding (algorithm e.g. hnsw, metric cosine) plus a standard text index on the feedback/text field for fast text filtering. Example index commands: db.customer_feedback.createIndex({ feedback_text: 'text' }, ...); db.customer_feedback.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { algorithm: 'hnsw', ...})
confusions.grounded_answer: Collection and field names are fine (customer_feedback, embedding). BUT the index creation must use DocumentDB's search/index APIs: text and vector indexes are created with `createSearchIndexes` and the vector index is a `vector-*` cosmosSearch subtype (e.g., `vector-hnsw` / `vector-diskann`) specified in the search index definition. Do not rely on a plain `createIndex({embedding:'vector'}, ...)` invocation.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer uses a MongoDB-style createIndex pattern for vectors and text; DocumentDB requires createSearchIndexes and `$search` usage for full-text and vector indexes.

confusion_sources.title: MongoDB Atlas vector / text examples that use createIndex

confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses createIndex for vectors or text, the indexes will not be created or used by DocumentDB's `$search` engine; search and vector queries will not return expected results.
improvements: Provide a small, copy-paste `runCommand({ createSearchIndexes: [...] })` index definition for the sample (text field + vector-diskann/hnsw index) in the sample repo README or a dedicated `indexes/create_indexes.json` file.
Document the embedding dimension in the README (once the embedding model/dimension is chosen) so the createSearchIndexes call includes correct `dimensions`.

confusions.question: What aggregation pipelines will surface net sentiment trends by channel, topic, and time?
confusions.cold_answer: Example aggregation pipelines ... group by channel/month compute avgSentiment and count; group by topic to compute avg sentiment and top quotes.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. Use MongoDB aggregation pipelines (e.g., $match, $group, $dateToString for monthly buckets, $sort, $limit) to compute average sentiment, counts and extract top quotes. DocumentDB supports aggregation pipeline stages; use explain() via the documentdb MCP `documentdb_explain_operation` tool to verify index usage.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none

confusions.question: What MCP/documentdb tooling will the sample use to verify collections, indexes and query plans?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (connection profile 'default') CLI/tools to inspect collections and indexes and to run explain plans on queries the sample creates.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. The `documentdb` MCP server (profile `default`) provides the necessary data-plane commands (list_databases, list_indexes, explain_operation, aggregate, find, insert) for verification.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none

information_gaps.title: Embedding model & vector dimension
information_gaps.description: The sample must pick an embedding provider and exact model (OpenAI/Azure OpenAI/other) which determines the embedding dimension (e.g., 1536 vs 384 vs 12288). Neither the installed skills nor Microsoft Learn provide project-specific model choices; the builder must choose model names and set EMBEDDING_MODEL and EMBEDDING_DIM env vars.

information_gaps.title: LLM model for extraction prompts
information_gaps.description: Which LLM (provider/model) the sample should use for the prompt-engineered extraction step (sentiment/topic/quote) is unspecified. This determines cost, latency and prompt design. The docs don't mandate a provider; include choices and env var names in the sample README.

information_gaps.title: Beanie compatibility with AsyncPyMongo
information_gaps.description: Skills documentdb-driver recommend AsyncPyMongo as the preferred async client, but Beanie historically depends on Motor. The DocumentDB skills do not say whether Beanie has a supported AsyncPyMongo backend or recommended adapter. Builder must decide and test which async client/ODM stack to use, or provide adapter code. Looked at: documentdb-driver skill, Beanie docs; no authoritative adapter guidance found.

information_gaps.title: Index parameter defaults for sample scale
information_gaps.description: Skills provide guidance on vector-index sub-types and tuning parameters (lBuild / lSearch / maxDegree), but the sample must choose defaults for the expected small seed dataset vs recommended production values. No single page prescribes sample defaults; the builder must choose based on embedding dimension and target vector-count and document that choice.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: When creating infrastructure or IaC for this sample, target resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts); use `az documentdb mongocluster` CLI or the mongoClusters Bicep module (see quickstarts).

sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Do not create vector / full-text indexes with the standard createIndex call; instead create search indexes via the `createSearchIndexes` DB command and query them via the `$search` aggregation stage; choose `vector-diskann` or `vector-hnsw` sub-type via documentdb-vector-search guidance and set `dimensions` to the chosen embedding model's output.

Read the cluster connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI (provided in the run environment) and set `retrywrites=false` and `tls=true` in client options; for Entra ID auth, follow the MONGODB-OIDC connection-string examples in the 'how to connect' docs.

sources.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using Microsoft Entra ID (how-to)

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Decide whether to use Beanie + Motor (simpler, historically supported) or migrate to PyMongo AsyncMongoClient per documentdb-driver guidance; document this choice in README and show the client singleton pattern for connection reuse.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample. The sample uses the provided cluster and az CLI; adding azd would help CI/CD but is not essential to build or verify the sample.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install Bicep on PATH if the builder wants to include the Bicep deployment variant or run the included Bicep-based deploy scripts locally. Install via Microsoft's guidance (az bicep install) or the Bicep release page. If not installed, the documentdb-azure-deployment skill provides an az resource create alternative for manual verification.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Add Terraform if the repository will include Terraform deployment examples. The documentdb-azure-deployment skill references AVM modules; without Terraform the builder must rely on Bicep/az CLI examples.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for the Python/Beanie LangChain sample. Add only if you plan to provide a .NET variant.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh to allow developers to run interactive checks (connect/ping, list collections, run explain) easily from the terminal. If it can't be added, the documentdb MCP server offers programmatic alternatives for the same checks.
